'''John William Townsend Jr.''' (1924 – October 29, 2011), known as '''Jack Townsend''', was an American physicist and [[Aerospace engineering|aerospace engineer]] who contributed to the development of the United States [[Space policy of the United States|space program]].

After the formation of [[NASA]] in 1958, he was among the first people to join NASA's [[Goddard Space Flight Center]] as assistant director in 1959 and was appointed its sixth director from 1987 to 1990. Townsend worked with [[James Van Allen]] on [[Sounding rocket|sounding rockets]] and was later involved in the creation of the world's first [[Weather satellite|weather]], [[Communications satellite|communications]], and [[Earth observation satellite|Earth observation satellites]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Logsdon |first1=John M. |last2=Launius |first2=Roger D. |last3=Onkst |first3=David H. |last4=Garber |first4=Stephen J. |title=Exploring the Unknown, Volume III: Using Space |date=1998 |publisher=NASA |location=Washington, D.C. |pages=155–159 |url=https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/sp-4407-etuv3.pdf?emrc=fe2581 |access-date=June 4, 2026}}</ref> He served as a presidential appointee at the [[Environmental Science Services Administration]] (ESSA) and the [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]] (NOAA) and held executive positions at [[Fairchild Industries]].

He was elected to the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 1975 and twice awarded the [[NASA Distinguished Service Medal]], the agency's highest honor.

==Early life and education==
Townsend was born and raised in [[Washington, D.C.]] in 1924.<ref>{{cite journal |title=ESSA deputy administrator named |journal=Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society |date=August 1968 |volume=49 |issue=8 |page=822 |url=https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/bams/49/8/1520-0477-49_8_822.pdf |access-date=June 19, 2026}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{cite web |title=Collection: John W. Townsend, Jr., Papers {{!}} ArchivesSpace Public Interface |url=https://aspace.lib.vt.edu/repositories/2/resources/1801 |website=aspace.lib.vt.edu |publisher=Virginia Institute of Technology |access-date=May 2, 2026}}</ref> He graduated from [[Jackson-Reed High School|Woodrow Wilson High School]] in 1942.<ref name=":wapo">{{cite news |last1=Langer |first1=Emily |title=John W. 'Jack' Townsend Jr., NASA physicist, dies |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/obituaries/john-w-jack-townsend-jr-nasa-physicist-dies/2011/11/16/gIQAJq0PSN_story.html |access-date=May 2, 2026 |work=The Washington Post |date=November 16, 2011}}</ref> An early interest in technology led him, at sixteen, to obtain a [[Pilot licensing and certification|pilot's license]] and an [[amateur radio]] license,<ref name=":wapo" /> and he maintained both for the rest of his life.<ref name=":2">{{cite web |title=Dr. John W. Townsend - NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/people/dr-john-w-townsend/ |publisher=NASA |access-date=May 2, 2026}}</ref>

During [[World War II]], he served in the [[United States Army Air Forces]] in the [[Pacific War|Pacific theater]], flying radar countermeasures aboard [[Boeing B-29 Superfortress|B-29]] bombers. After the war, he enrolled at [[Williams College]] in Massachusetts, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts and a Master of Arts in physics.<ref name=":3">{{cite news |title=Former Goddard Center Director John Townsend Dead at 87 |url=https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/former-goddard-center-director-john-townsend-dead-at-87-133378483.html |access-date=May 2, 2026 |via=PR Newswire |publisher=NASA |date=November 7, 2011 |language=en}}</ref> The college later awarded him an [[Honorary degree|honorary]] [[Doctor of Science]] degree.<ref name=":2" />

==Career==

===Naval Research Laboratory===
In 1949, Townsend joined the [[United States Naval Research Laboratory]] (NRL) working on the nascent American [[sounding rocket]] program at [[White Sands Missile Range]] in New Mexico as a research physicist.<ref name=":3" /> He instrumented [[V-2]] rockets captured from Germany at the end of the war and began working on sounding rockets like [[Viking (rocket)|Viking]] for upper-atmosphere research.<ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=Dr. John W. Townsend Jr. {{!}} National Air and Space Museum |url=https://airandspace.si.edu/support/wall-of-honor/dr-john-w-townsend-jr |website=airandspace.si.edu |publisher=Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum |access-date=May 2, 2026}}</ref> 

Throughout the 1950s, he worked on the [[Aerobee]] sounding rocket with [[Eleanor C. Pressly]] and James Van Allen, who had initiated the Aerobee's development at the [[Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory|Applied Physics Laboratory]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Van Allen |first1=J. A. |last2=Fraser |first2=L. W. |last3=Floyd |first3=J. F. R. |title=The Aerobee Sounding Rocket: A New Vehicle for Research in the Upper Atmosphere |journal=Science |volume=108 |pages=746–747 |doi= 10.1126/science.108.2818.746 |date=1948}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=James Alfred Van Allen |journal=Physics Today |doi=10.1063/1.2435692 |url=https://physicstoday.aip.org/obituaries/james-alfred-van-allen |access-date=June 19, 2026|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Corliss |first1=William R. |title=NASA Sounding Rockets, 1958-1966: A Historical Summary |date=1971 |publisher=NASA Scientific and Technical Information Office |location=Washington, D.C. |pages=18; 20 |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19720005224/downloads/19720005224.pdf |access-date=June 5, 2026}}</ref> Townsend published a book chapter on the vehicle with Van Allen and Pressly in 1959.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Van Allen |first1=James A. |last2=Townsend, Jr. |first2=John W. |last3=Pressly |first3=Eleanor C. |last4=Newell, Jr. |first4=Homer E. |title=Sounding Rockets, Chapter 4: The Aerobee Rocket |date=January 1, 1959 |publisher=McGraw-Hill |location=New York |pages=55-70}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=James Van Allen Publications: No. 67 |url=https://space.physics.uiowa.edu/plasma-wave/ProfVanAllen/vanallen_publications.html |website=space.physics.uiowa.edu |publisher=University of Iowa |access-date=June 11, 2026}}</ref> The Aerobee was the United States' primary suborbital research rocket, first launched in late 1947.<ref name=":6">{{cite web |last1=Ludwig |first1=George H. |title=James Alfred Van Allen. From High School to the Beginning of the Space Era:  A Biographical Sketch (2004) |url=https://space.physics.uiowa.edu/plasma-wave/van90/VanAllenBio_LudwigOct2004.pdf |website=p. 5 |publisher=University of Iowa |access-date=June 5, 2026}}</ref> Over the following decades it flew numerous missions across multiple variants<ref>{{cite book |last1=Busse |first1=Jon R. |last2=Leffler |first2=Merril T. |last3=Administration |first3=United States National Aeronautics and Space |title=A Compendium of Aerobee Sounding Rocket Launchings from 1959 Through 1963 |date=1966 |publisher=National Aeronautics and Space Administration |page=153 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/A_Compendium_of_Aerobee_Sounding_Rocket/VewQAQAAIAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=aerobee+rocket&printsec=frontcover |access-date=June 5, 2026 |language=en}}</ref> studying [[atmospheric physics]], astronomy, [[Cosmic ray|cosmic rays]], and related phenomena from altitudes typically ranging between 40 and 65 miles.<ref name=":6" /> Its highest recorded flight, in June 1955, exceeded 91 miles.<ref name=":6" /> 

The test flights allowed Townsend to develop [[mass spectrometry]] using [[radio]] frequencies.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Townsend |first1=J. W. |title=Radiofrequency Mass Spectrometer for Upper Air Research |journal=Review of Scientific Instruments |date=October 1, 1952 |volume=23 |issue=10 |pages=538–541 |doi=10.1063/1.1746079 |url=https://pubs.aip.org/aip/rsi/article-abstract/23/10/538/297908/Radiofrequency-Mass-Spectrometer-for-Upper-Air?redirectedFrom=PDF |access-date=June 5, 2026|url-access=subscription }}</ref> As part of studies conducted for the [[Naval Research Laboratory]], he measured data on atmospheric gas from rockets flown over the [[upper atmosphere]] over [[White Sands Missile Range]] and the [[subarctic]] town of [[Churchill, Manitoba]],<ref>{{cite book |last1=Newell |first1=Homer Edward |title=Beyond the Atmosphere: Early Years of Space Science |date=1980 |publisher=Scientific and Technical Information Branch, National Aeronautics and Space Administration |location=Washington, D.C. |page=79 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Beyond_the_Atmosphere/NkICAAAAIAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=0 |access-date=June 5, 2026|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Henry 1958"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Townsend, Jr. |first1=J. W. |last2=Meadows |first2=E. B. |last3=Pressly |first3=E. C. |title=Composition of the Upper Atmosphere |journal=World Data Center A |date=1954 |issue=IGY Rocket Report No. 6 |pages=61-82}}</ref> though he advised that the two places were too small a sample size to reliably calculate the atmosphere throughout the entire Earth.<ref name="Henry 1958">{{cite news |last=Henry |first=Thomas R. |date=November 21, 1958 |title=Vistas in Science |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/evening-star-vistas-in-science/199918452/ |work=Evening Star |page=20 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> Cameras mounted on [[Nike-Cajun]] rocket photographed the Earth during ascent;<ref>{{cite web |last1=Corliss |first1=William R. |title=NASA Sounding Rockets, 1958–1968: A Historical Summary |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19720005224/downloads/19720005224.pdf |publisher=NASA Historical Report Series |date=1971 |access-date=May 2, 2026}}</ref> these images later drew the attention of meteorologist [[Harry Wexler]] at the [[United States Weather Bureau]] and contributed to early discussions about orbital weather observation.<ref name="ams-townsend">{{cite web |title=Jack Townsend, Shepherd of Weather Satellite Technology |url=https://blog.ametsoc.org/2011/11/08/jack-townsend-shepherd-of-weather-satellite-technology/ |website=The Front Page |publisher=American Meteorological Society |date=November 8, 2011 |access-date=June 19, 2026}}</ref>

===Goddard Space Flight Center===
With the establishment of NASA in 1958, both the [[Project Vanguard|Vanguard Project]] and Townsend's NRL branch were folded into the new agency by President [[Dwight D. Eisenhower]],<ref name=":8">{{cite book |last1=Newell |first1=Homer Edward |title=Beyond the Atmosphere: Early Years of Space Science |date=1980 |publisher=Scientific and Technical Information Branch, National Aeronautics and Space Administration |location=Washington, D.C. |page=105 |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19810012433/downloads/19810012433.pdf |access-date=June 10, 2026 |language=en}}</ref> and Townsend took charge of the Space Sciences Division.<ref name=":3" /> He was one of the earliest people to work at the newly opened Goddard Space Flight Center in [[Greenbelt, Maryland]], joining in 1959 as the center's acting director until [[Harry J. Goett]] was appointed director in September 1959,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Newell |first1=Homer Edward |title=Beyond the Atmosphere: Early Years of Space Science |date=1980 |publisher=Scientific and Technical Information Branch, National Aeronautics and Space Administration |location=Washington, D.C. |page=250 |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19810012433/downloads/19810012433.pdf |access-date=June 10, 2026 |language=en}}</ref> after which Townsend continued as assistant director for Space Science and Satellite Applications.<ref name=":2" />

Townsend was chosen as acting director because his ties with figures from the NRL, including [[John F. Clark (engineer)|John F. Clark]] and as deputy under [[Homer E. Newell Jr.]], helped ease early friction between Goddard and [[NASA Headquarters]].<ref name=":9">{{cite book |last1=Newell |first1=Homer Edward |title=Beyond the Atmosphere: Early Years of Space Science |date=1980 |publisher=Scientific and Technical Information Branch, National Aeronautics and Space Administration |location=Washington, D.C. |pages=250-253 |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19810012433/downloads/19810012433.pdf |access-date=June 9, 2026 |language=en}}</ref> When a dispute arose between the two centers over the boundary between program and project management, Townsend, then Goett's senior official for space science, argued that programs containing only a single project made the boundary unworkable.<ref name=":9" /> He recommended grouping several projects under each program manager, an approach Newell and his deputy [[Edgar Cortright]] agreed to adopt.<ref name=":9" />
[[File:Russian Scientists from the Commission of Interplanetary Travel of the Soviet Academy of Science Visit Langley Research Center - LRC-1959-B701 P-08164.jpg|thumb|Townsend (back row, left) with Soviet scientists including [[Leonid Sedov]] and [[Anatoly Blagonravov]] in 1959]]
[[Frank B. McDonald|Frank McDonald]], a NASA scientist who worked closely with Townsend, credited him with helping choose the Greenbelt site and guiding the research the new center would pursue.<ref name=":wapo" /> Townsend built up a group devoted to spacecraft fabrication and led the scientists responsible for its launch vehicles.<ref name=":wapo" /> Newell later wrote that Townsend aided Goett in "building up Goddard" and "launching their initial projects".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Newell |first1=Homer Edward |title=Beyond the Atmosphere: Early Years of Space Science |date=1980 |publisher=Scientific and Technical Information Branch, National Aeronautics and Space Administration |location=Washington, D.C. |page=251 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Beyond_the_Atmosphere/NkICAAAAIAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&bsq=townsend |access-date=June 5, 2026 |language=en}}</ref> 

Townsend was involved in the development of early meteorological, communications, and Earth-viewing satellite systems.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{cite book |last1=Logsdon |first1=John M. |last2=Launius |first2=Roger D. |last3=Onkst |first3=David H. |last4=Garber |first4=Stephen J. |title=Exploring the Unknown, Volume III: Using Space |date=1998 |publisher=NASA |location=Washington, D.C. |pages=498–501 |url=https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/sp-4308.pdf |access-date=June 4, 2026}}</ref> One of the satellites developed at Goddard, TIROS-1, was launched in April 1960 and became the world's first successful [[weather satellite]].<ref name="tiros1-nasa">{{cite web |title=Launch of TIROS 1, World's 1st Weather Satellite — This Week in Goddard History |url=https://www.nasa.gov/history/launch-of-tiros-1-worlds-1st-weather-satellite-this-week-in-goddard-history-march-31-april-6/ |publisher=NASA |access-date=June 19, 2026}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> He was appointed deputy director of Goddard in 1965, a post he held until 1968, during which time he pressed for institutional investment in astronomy, [[solar physics]], and related space sciences.<ref name=":wapo" /><ref>{{cite book |last1=Baker |first1=David |title=The Rocket: The History and Development of Rocket & Missile Technology |date=1978 |publisher=Crown |isbn=978-0-517-53404-5 |page=140 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Rocket/hEE-AQAAIAAJ |language=en}}</ref> He was also called to testify about [[Sputnik 3]] during the [[Sputnik crisis]], as noted by the [[Central Intelligence Agency|CIA]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lowrance |first=V. L. |date=September 10, 1958 |title=Briefing on Sputnik III |url=https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/docs/CIA-RDP61S00750A000500070013-4.pdf |url-status=live |website=CIA.gov |publisher=Office of the Chief of Naval Operations, Department of the Navy |place=Washington, D.C.|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250304002637/https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/docs/CIA-RDP61S00750A000500070013-4.pdf|archive-date=2025-03-04}}</ref>

He also served on a three-person presidential commission that negotiated early agreements with the [[Soviet Union]] on the peaceful and civilian uses of outer space,<ref name=":2" /> including arrangements for the international exchange of meteorological satellite data.<ref name=":0" />

===NOAA and federal service===
In 1968, Townsend was named the deputy administrator of the [[Environmental Science Services Administration]] (ESSA) by President [[Lyndon B. Johnson]].<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":0" /> In July 1970, he briefed the [[Senate Commerce Committee]]'s subcommittee for oceanography on Reorganization Plan No.4,<ref>{{cite journal |title=Reorganization plan 4 of 1970 to create a National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration in the Department of Commerce. |journal=Hearing before the Subcommittee on Oceanography of the Committee on Commerce, United States Senate, Ninety-First Congress, Second Session. |date=July 27, 1970 |pages=1-3 |url=https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CHRG-91shrg50931/pdf/CHRG-91shrg50931.pdf |access-date=June 10, 2026}}</ref> a proposal to consolidate the ESSA with the [[Bureau of Commercial Fisheries]] and other federal marine programs into a single agency.<ref>{{cite web |title=Title 5, Appendix—Reorganization Plan No. 4 of 1970 |url=https://darrp.noaa.gov/sites/default/files/Reorganization%20Plan%20No.%204%20of%201970.pdf |publisher=NOAA |access-date=June 10, 2026}}</ref> The plan took effect in October 1970, with the creation of the [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]] (NOAA). The ESSA was the largest constituent, with almost 10,000 civil servants forming two-thirds of the new agency.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Shea |first1=Eileen L. |title=A History of NOAA: Being a Compilation of Facts and Figures Regarding the Life and Times of the Original Whole Earth Agency |date=1987 |publisher=Department of Commerce, Historical Council |location=Washington, D.C. |page=3 |url=https://www.noaa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-07/shea_history_NOAA.pdf |access-date=June 10, 2026}}</ref> President [[Richard Nixon]] appointed him NOAA's associate administrator, serving under [[Robert M. White (meteorologist)|Robert M. White]], with whom he had led ESSA.<ref>{{cite book |title=Memorial Tributes: Volume 20 |chapter=Robert M. White |date=2016 |publisher=The National Academies Press |location=Washington, D.C. |doi=10.17226/23394 |chapter-url=https://nap.nationalacademies.org/read/23394/chapter/61 |access-date=June 9, 2026}}</ref><ref name=":2" /> He served in the position until 1977.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4">{{cite web |title=Chapter 2: Seeking Government Support for a Satellite Program |url=https://www.nasa.gov/history/sputnik/chapter2.html |publisher=NASA |access-date=May 2, 2026}}</ref>

The new agency combined organizations with long-separate histories and institutional culture. He responded to concerns raised by Senator [[Mike Gravel]] and conservation groups that fisheries programs would be marginalized within a commerce-oriented agency.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Reorganization plan 4 of 1970 to create a National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration in the Department of Commerce. |journal=Hearing before the Subcommittee on Oceanography of the Committee on Commerce, United States Senate, Ninety-First Congress, Second Session. |date=July 27, 1970 |pages=2-4 |url=https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CHRG-91shrg50931/pdf/CHRG-91shrg50931.pdf |access-date=June 10, 2026}}</ref> During this nine-year period of leadership, he was involved in developing operational meteorological [[Polar orbit|polar orbiting]] and [[Geostationary orbit|geostationary]] satellite systems. The joint NASA–NOAA geostationary experiments begun under ESSA became operational with the launch of the [[Synchronous Meteorological Satellite]] in 1974–1975 and of [[GOES-1]], NOAA's first geostationary satellite, in October 1975.<ref name=":10">{{cite book |last1=Shea |first1=Eileen L. |title=A History of NOAA: Being a Compilation of Facts and Figures Regarding the Life and Times of the Original Whole Earth Agency |date=1987 |publisher=Department of Commerce, Historical Council |location=Washington, D.C. |pages=14; 28 |url=https://www.noaa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-07/shea_history_NOAA.pdf |access-date=June 10, 2026}}</ref> In recognition of this work, the [[National Academy of Engineering]] elected him as a member in 1975.<ref name=":5">{{cite web |title=Dr. John W. Townsend Jr. |url=https://www.nae.edu/28441/Dr-John-W-Townsend-Jr |publisher=National Academy of Engineering |access-date=May 2, 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

===Private sector===

After leaving federal service in the late 1970s, Townsend moved into the private aerospace industry.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4">{{cite web |title=Chapter 2: Seeking Government Support for a Satellite Program |url=https://www.nasa.gov/history/sputnik/chapter2.html |publisher=NASA |access-date=May 2, 2026}}</ref> He served as President of the space division of [[Fairchild Industries]] and subsequently rose to Executive Vice President of the parent company, a position he held until 1987.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{cite news |last1=Langer |first1=Emily |title=John W. ‘Jack’ Townsend Jr., NASA physicist, dies |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/obituaries/john-w-jack-townsend-jr-nasa-physicist-dies/2011/11/16/gIQAJq0PSN_story.html |access-date=May 2, 2026 |work=The Washington Post |date=November 16, 2011}}</ref>
===Return to NASA and Goddard directorship===
Following the [[Space Shuttle Challenger disaster]] in January 1986, NASA Administrator [[James C. Fletcher|James Fletcher]] called on Townsend and other experienced former officials to assist the agency. Townsend worked at NASA headquarters during the period preceding the Space Shuttle's return to flight.<ref name=":2" /> On June 22, 1987, he was appointed Director of Goddard Space Flight Center, succeeding [[Noel Hinners]].<ref>{{cite book |title=NASA Activities |date=1988 |publisher=The Administration |page=29 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/NASA_Activities/IRBSvDWthI8C?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=john+w.+townsend+jr+june+22+1987&pg=PA29&printsec=frontcover |access-date=May 2, 2026 |language=en}}</ref> 

During his three years as director, the center delivered several achievements central to NASA's recovery from the Challenger accident. The Space Shuttle returned to flight in September 1988 with the [[STS-26]] mission, which deployed a Tracking and Data Relay Satellite (TDRS-3), restoring the Goddard-managed [[Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System]] after the loss of a second satellite aboard Challenger.<ref>{{cite web |title=35 Years Ago: STS-26 Returns the Space Shuttle to Flight |url=https://www.nasa.gov/history/35-years-ago-sts-26-returns-the-space-shuttle-to-flight/ |publisher=NASA |date=September 29, 2023 |access-date=July 9, 2026}}</ref> In November 1989, Goddard launched the [[Cosmic Background Explorer]] (COBE), a satellite built in-house at the center that had been redesigned in under three years to fly on a [[Delta (rocket family)|Delta rocket]] after the Challenger accident eliminated its planned Space Shuttle launch. COBE's measurements of the [[cosmic microwave background]] provided evidence for the [[Big Bang]], which physicist [[Stephen Hawking]] called "the discovery of the century, if not of all time."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Wallace |first1=Lane E. |title=Dreams, Hopes, Realities: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, The First Forty Years |date=1999 |publisher=NASA History Office, National Aeronautics and Space Administration |location=Washington, D.C. |pages=43–44 |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19990054617/downloads/19990054617.pdf |access-date=July 9, 2026 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=COBE Satellite Marks 20th Anniversary |url=https://www.nasa.gov/universe/cobe-satellite-marks-20th-anniversary/ |publisher=NASA |access-date=July 9, 2026}}</ref> Goddard also managed development of the Hubble Space Telescope's scientific instruments and its mission operations ahead of the telescope's launch in April 1990.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Wallace |first1=Lane E. |title=Dreams, Hopes, Realities: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, The First Forty Years |date=1999 |publisher=NASA History Office, National Aeronautics and Space Administration |location=Washington, D.C. |pages=34–35, 43 |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19990054617/downloads/19990054617.pdf |access-date=July 9, 2026 |language=en}}</ref> 

He retired on June 30, 1990, and was succeeded by [[John M. Klineberg]].<ref>{{cite web |title=John M. Klineberg - NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/people/john-m-klineberg/ |publisher=National Aeronautics and Space Administration |access-date=June 19, 2026}}</ref>

==Later life and legacy==
After retiring, Townsend remained active in advisory and scientific capacities. He chaired the [[National Research Council (United States)|National Research Council]]'s Space Applications Board and contributed to scientific studies undertaken by the National Academies and other bodies, including a report on low-altitude wind shear and aviation safety.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" /> In 1982, following the crash of [[Pan Am Flight 759]] in a [[downburst]], Congress directed the [[Federal Aviation Administration]] to commission a National Academy of Sciences study of wind shear hazards.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Feaver |first1=Douglas B. |title=The Wind Shear Risk: Cost vs. Safety |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/1985/08/18/the-wind-shear-risk-cost-vs-safety/7e98bfb9-2e73-4444-9268-2e29c209d797 |access-date=June 19, 2026 |work=The Washington Post |date=August 18, 1985}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Sullivan |first1=Walter |title=New Study of Downdrafts Expected to Reduce Danger of Plane Crashes |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1982/07/20/science/new-study-of-downdrafts-expected-to-reduce-danger-of-plane-crashes.html |access-date=June 9, 2026 |work=The New York Times |date=July 20, 1982}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Aircraft Accident Report Pan American World Airways, Inc., Clipper 759, Boeing 727-235, No 4737, New Orleans International Airport  Kenner, Louisiana |journal=National Transportation Safety Board |date=July 9, 1982 |pages=74-75 |url=https://www.fss.aero/accident-reports/dvdfiles/US/1982-07-09-US.pdf |access-date=June 19, 2026}}</ref> Townsend chaired the committee<ref name=":2" /> whose 1983 report confirmed low-altitude wind shear as a significant hazard to aircraft during takeoff and landing.<ref name=":7">{{cite journal |title=Low-Altitude Wind Shear and its Hazard to Aviation |journal=National Research Council |date=January 1, 1983 |doi=10.17226/558 |url=https://www.nationalacademies.org/publications/558 |access-date=June 9, 2026|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The report recommended better detection and increased [[pilot training]].<ref name=":7" />

He served on panels including the NASA Advisory Council, the Advisory Board Panel on International Cooperation and Competition in Civilian Space Activities at the Office of Technology Assessment, and the [[International Academy of Astronautics]].<ref name=":2" />

Townsend died on October 29, 2011, at [[Sibley Memorial Hospital]] in Washington, D.C., from complications of [[lung cancer]], at the age of 87.<ref>{{cite news |title=John Townsend, 87, Ran NASA's Goddard Center |url=https://spacenews.com/john-townsend-87-ran-nasas-goddard-center/ |access-date=May 2, 2026 |work=Space News |date=November 7, 2011}}</ref> 

Upon his death, Goddard Director [[Rob Strain]] said that Townsend had been "truly one of the seminal figures in the history of NASA, and certainly, in the history of Goddard," adding that a history of the American space program "simply could not be written without a chapter devoted to him."<ref name=":2" />

==Personal life==
Townsend's hobbies included [[Steam-powered vessel|live steam]] [[Rail transport modelling|rail model]]s, [[orchid]]-growing, and sailing.<ref name=":arrl"/> He held an amateur radio license from the age of 16,<ref name=":wapo" /> operating under the callsign W3PRB for more than six decades, and was a member of the [[American Radio Relay League]].<ref name=":arrl">{{cite web |title=Space Pioneer Jack Townsend, W3PRB (SK) |url=https://www.arrl.org/news/space-pioneer-jack-townsend-w3prb-sk |website=www.arrl.org |publisher=National Association for Amateur Radio (ARRL) |access-date=May 2, 2026 |language=en}}</ref> 

He had three children with his first wife, Mary Lewis Townsend, who died in 1986 following a 38-year marriage, and he later married JoAnn Clayton Townsend.<ref name=":wapo" /><ref>{{cite news |title=Deaths Elsewhere |url=https://bendbulletin.com/2011/11/18/deaths-elsewhere-265/ |access-date=May 2, 2026 |work=The Bulletin |date=November 18, 2011 |language=en}}</ref>
